candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 22 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 23 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 24 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 25 not required. 26
candidates.context: This guidance provides recommendations to industry on conducting risk evaluation and 16 mitigation strategies (REMS) assessment surveys, used to evaluate respondent knowledge of 17 REMS-related information. This guidance discusses general principles and recommendations 18 related to conducting REMS assessment knowledge surveys, including study design, survey 19 instrument development, survey data collection and processing, and data analysis. 20

candidates.statement: Since it is rarely possible to survey the entire target population of those who take a drug, or those 186 who prescribe or dispense a drug, sampling of the target population is more feasible. REMS 187 assessment knowledge surveys should be based on the principle of statistical inference, which 188 generalizes findings from a sample to a target population. 17 The generalizability of the survey 189 results to the target population is based on how representative the sample is of the target 190 population. 191
candidates.context: B. Sampling Considerations 184 An initial step in designing the survey is identifying a sampling frame of the target population. 193 That is, a list of those in the target population from which the sample can be selected. Examples 194 of sampling frames for a REMS target population include individuals in a REMS-mandated 195 patient registry, patient enrollment database, or prescriber or pharmacy enrollment database. 196 When a REMS does not include mandatory databases, possible sampling frames of patients and 197 healthcare providers could be chain pharmacies, voluntary patient registries, or other sources. It 198 is important to provide the rationale for choosing the selected sampling frame that takes into 199 consideration the representativeness of the sampling frame relative to the target population. 200 Evaluating representativeness of a survey sample of the target population include

candidates.statement: In this section, sample size refers to the number of survey participants in a population of interest. 278 The number of subjects invited to participate in a survey should be larger than the target sample 279 size to account for nonresponse. 280
candidates.context: C. Sample Size Considerations 276 For a given target population, we recommend that the sample be large enough to precisely 282 estimate the knowledge rate in that population. Sample size calculation considers two important 283 elements: sampling design (see section III.B, above) and precision of the estimated knowledge 284 rate. This guidance discusses three sampling designs: SRS, cluster sample, and stratified 285 random sample. 286

candidates.statement: The design effect of a survey design is the ratio of the variance of estimates from that design, 323 divided by the variance of estimates from an SRS of the same size. For example, when the 324 design effect is 2, the sample size should be twice as large as an SRS survey to achieve the same 325 target precision. Conversely, when the design effect is 0.5, the sample size can be half the size of 326 an SRS survey to achieve the same target precision. 327
candidates.context: For a clustered design, a stratified random sample, or other complex designs, the sample size to 321 achieve a certain precision differs from the sample size in a SRS by the design effect factor. 23 The appropriate sample size to achieve a certain precision is higher in a cluster design than in an 329 SRS by the design effect factor because the variance of estimates in the cluster design is higher 330 than in an SRS (i.e., design effect factor > 1). 24 The design effect in a cluster design increases 331 with the number of subjects in each cluster and with intra-cluster correlation coefficients (ICC) 25 . 332
